entries.originalText: O Lord, I still need more grace, if I would arrive where neither man nor any other creature may hinder me.
entries.modernizedText: O Lord, I still need more grace, if I would arrive where neither man nor any other creature may hinder me.

entries.originalText: For so long as anything keepeth me back, I cannot freely fly unto Thee.
entries.modernizedText: For so long as anything keeps me back, I cannot freely fly to You.

entries.originalText: He desired eagerly thus to fly, who cried, saying, Oh that I had wings like a dove, for then would I flee away and be at rest.
entries.modernizedText: He desired eagerly to fly thus, who cried, saying, Oh that I had wings like a dove, for then would I flee away and be at rest.

entries.originalText: What is more peaceful than the single eye?
entries.modernizedText: What is more peaceful than the single eye?

entries.originalText: And what more free than he that desireth nothing upon earth?
entries.modernizedText: And what more free than he who desires nothing upon earth?

entries.originalText: Therefore must a man rise above every creature, and perfectly forsake himself, and with abstracted mind to stand and behold that Thou, the Creator of all things, hast among Thy creatures nothing like unto Thyself.
entries.modernizedText: Therefore a man must rise above every creature, and perfectly forsake himself, and with a mind withdrawn from other things stand and behold that You, the Creator of all things, have among Your creatures nothing like Yourself.

entries.originalText: And except a man be freed from all creatures, he will not be able to reach freely after Divine things.
entries.modernizedText: And unless a man is freed from all creatures, he will not be able to reach freely after Divine things.

entries.originalText: Therefore few are found who give themselves to contemplation, because few know how to separate themselves entirely from perishing and created things.
entries.modernizedText: Therefore few are found who give themselves to contemplation, because few know how to separate themselves entirely from perishing and created things.

entries.originalText: For this much grace is necessary, which may lift up the soul and raise it above itself.
entries.modernizedText: For this much grace is necessary, which may lift up the soul and raise it above itself.

entries.originalText: And except a man be lifted up in the spirit, and freed from all creatures, and altogether united to God, whatsoever he knoweth, whatsoever even he hath, it mattereth but little.
entries.modernizedText: And unless a man is lifted up in the spirit, and freed from all creatures, and altogether united to God, whatever he knows, whatever even he has, it matters but little.

entries.originalText: He who esteemeth anything great save the one only incomprehensible, eternal, good, shall long time be little and lie low.
entries.modernizedText: He who esteems anything great except the one only incomprehensible, eternal, good, will long be little and lie low.

entries.originalText: For whatsoever is not God is nothing, and ought to be counted for nothing.
entries.modernizedText: For whatever is not God is nothing, and ought to be counted for nothing.

entries.originalText: Great is the difference between a godly man, illuminated with wisdom, and a scholar learned in knowledge and given to books.
entries.modernizedText: Great is the difference between a godly man, illuminated with wisdom, and a scholar learned in knowledge and given to books.

entries.originalText: Far nobler is that doctrine which floweth down from the divine fulness above, than that which is acquired laboriously by human study.
entries.modernizedText: Far nobler is that doctrine which flows down from the divine fullness above, than that which is acquired laboriously by human study.

entries.originalText: Many are found who desire contemplation, but they do not strive to practice those things which are required thereunto.
entries.modernizedText: Many are found who desire contemplation, but they do not strive to practice those things which are required for it.

entries.originalText: It is also a great impediment, that much is made of symbols and external signs, and too little of thorough mortification.
entries.modernizedText: It is also a great impediment that much is made of symbols and external signs, and too little of thorough mortification.

entries.originalText: I know not how it is, and by what spirit we are led, and what we who would be deemed spiritual are aiming at, that we give so great labour and so eager solicitude for transitory and worthless things, and scarcely ever gather our senses together to think at all of our inward condition.
entries.modernizedText: I do not know how it is, and by what spirit we are led, and what we who would be considered spiritual are aiming at, that we give so great labor and so eager concern to transitory and worthless things, and scarcely ever gather our senses together to think at all of our inward condition.

entries.originalText: Ah, me!
entries.modernizedText: Ah, me!

entries.originalText: Forthwith after a little recollection we rush out of doors, and do not subject our actions to a strict examination.
entries.modernizedText: Immediately after a little recollection we rush out of doors, and do not subject our actions to a strict examination.

entries.originalText: Where our affections are set we take no heed, and we weep not that all things belonging to us are so defiled.
entries.modernizedText: We take no heed where our affections are set, and we do not weep that all things belonging to us are so defiled.

entries.originalText: For because all flesh had corrupted itself upon the earth, the great deluge came.
entries.modernizedText: For because all flesh had corrupted itself upon the earth, the great deluge came.

entries.originalText: Since therefore our inmost affections are very corrupt, it followeth of necessity that our actions also are corrupt, being the index of a deficient inward strength.
entries.modernizedText: Since therefore our inmost affections are very corrupt, it follows of necessity that our actions also are corrupt, being the index of a deficient inward strength.

entries.originalText: Out of a pure heart proceedeth the fruit of good living.
entries.modernizedText: Out of a pure heart proceeds the fruit of good living.

entries.originalText: We demand, how much a man hath done; but from how much virtue he acted, is not so narrowly considered.
entries.modernizedText: We demand how much a man has done; but from how much virtue he acted is not so closely considered.

entries.originalText: We ask if he be strong, rich, handsome, clever, whether he is a good writer, good singer, good workman; but how poor he may be in spirit, how patient and gentle, how devout and meditative, on these things many are silent.
entries.modernizedText: We ask if he is strong, rich, handsome, clever, whether he is a good writer, good singer, good workman; but how poor he may be in spirit, how patient and gentle, how devout and meditative, on these things many are silent.

entries.originalText: Nature looketh upon the outward appearance of a man, grace turneth its thought to the heart.
entries.modernizedText: Nature looks upon the outward appearance of a man; grace turns its thought to the heart.

entries.originalText: The former frequently judgeth amiss; the latter trusteth in God, that it may not be deceived.
entries.modernizedText: The former frequently judges wrongly; the latter trusts in God, that it may not be deceived.
